summary:
The Silent Scouts:Postcards from Beyond Earth is an interactive web app designed for students aged 7–13. Users adjust a simulated Deep Space Network radio tuner across the Moon, Mars, and deep space to catch first-person transmissions from 11 real NASA spacecraft—from the Apollo 11 laser mirrors and Opportunity rover to Pioneer 10. Each postcard pairs custom vector schematics and verified NASA NSSDCA telemetry with browser voice synthesis, two reading levels, and a short quiz that awards stamps in a digital logbook.  
Since the 1960s, NASA has left dozens of rovers, landers, and probes across the Solar System, yet their records sit inside dense technical databases that young students rarely read. Retired spacecraft are often dismissed as "space junk" instead of being understood as working machines that answered major questions about our universe.  
Built for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, the app connects each spacecraft's real engineering design to the scientific discoveries it enabled. For example, users learn how Opportunity's solar arrays survived Martian dust for nearly 15 years to find water-formed minerals, or why Ingenuity's carbon blades spun at 2500 RPM to achieve the first flight on another planet.  
By running directly in any browser without installation, the app gives classrooms and families a simple tool to explore space history. Showing kids how past engineering solved real cosmic problems encourages them to become the builders of future missions.
details:
What It Does & How It Works
The Silent Scouts: Postcards from Beyond Earth is a single-page web app for kids aged 7–13. Users adjust a Deep Space Signal Tuner (via band buttons or a slider) to switch between three zones: The Moon (1.3 light-seconds delay), Mars (4–24 light-minutes), and Deep Space (up to 22+ light-hours). Moving the tuner updates live physics facts about light-speed radio delays and filters the spacecraft located in each region.
Clicking any of the 11 spacecraft cards (Apollo 11 Eagle & ALSEP, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, Kepler, and others) opens a modal window with:
* NSSDCA Mission Specs: International designator IDs, active dates, coordinates, power source, and dry mass.
* First-Person Postcards: Stories written from the robot's point of view, with a toggle between Junior Cadet (7–9) and Specialist (10–13) reading levels.
* Audio Playback: A Listen to Postcard button that reads the story aloud using browser speech synthesis.
* Engineering → Science Link: A short explanation of how the spacecraft's hardware led to real scientific discoveries.
* Quiz & Logbook: A quick question on each card that unlocks Archivist Stamps, saved in the Junior Space Archivist Logbook.
Benefits & Intended Impact
Space archives store mission records in dense tables that kids rarely read, so retired probes often get forgotten as "space junk". Turning those records into an interactive radio tuner makes space history easier to explore at school or at home. Seeing how past engineering solved real off-world problems helps spark curiosity in science and future space missions.
Tools & Technologies Used
* Code & Styling: Single-file HTML5, vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), custom CSS, Tailwind CSS (CDN), and Google Fonts (Inter, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono).
* Graphics, Audio & Data: Custom inline SVG schematics for each spacecraft, an HTML5 Canvas starfield, the browser's window.speechSynthesis API for voice playback, localStorage to save earned stamps without a backend, and mission telemetry from the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA).
Creativity & Design Considerations
Instead of building a plain list or timeline, we designed the screen like a Deep Space Network radio console. We focused on three practical goals: making it a standalone HTML file that runs in any browser with zero setup, supporting both younger and older kids through dual reading levels and voice audio, and keeping every number and physics detail faithful to real NSSDCA records.Artificial Intelligence (SI) tools were used to generate the source code, layout, and geometric vector elements representing satellites on our website.
